label: Community Rule 1QS (Serekh HaYakhad) — Complete
summary_plain: The Community Rule governs the covenant community at Qumran. Those who enter the covenant commit to seek YHWH with all their heart and soul, to do what is good and upright before him, and to walk no more in the stubbornness of a guilty heart. New members undergo examination and a two-year probationary period. The community practices common meals, common prayer, and nightly Torah study. The Two Spirits doctrine teaches that YHWH created two spirits — the Spirit of Truth and the Spirit of Deceit — and all humanity walks in their ways. The community is governed by the sons of Tzadok and by the council of the community. The rule concludes with a hymn praising YHWH’s righteousness.
summary_scholarly: The Community Rule (1QS — Serekh HaYakhad) was among the first seven scrolls found in Cave 1 in 1947. It is the foundational governance document of the Qumran community. The text includes: entry procedures and oath formulas (Col I-III), the Two Spirits doctrine (Col III:13-IV:26), community discipline and hierarchy (Col V-IX), and a closing hymn (Col X-XI). The Two Spirits doctrine is a dualistic theological framework unlike anything in the Masoretic canon — YHWH created both spirits and appointed them until the final visitation. The community structure presupposes a functioning alternative society with its own legal system, calendar, and liturgy. Multiple copies were found in Cave 4 (4Q255-264, 4Q280, 4Q286-287), showing the text’s central importance.

key_terms.definition: The Community Rule — the foundational governing document of the Qumran Yahad found in Cave 1 (1QS) and six Cave 4 copies. Contains the entry rite, the Two Spirits doctrine, the penal code, the Maskil's hymn, and the community's covenant identity.

Unity / together — the name the Qumran community used for itself. 'The community of the Yakhad.' Members were called 'men of the Yakhad.' Yakhad signifies total communal commitment: shared property, shared meals, shared purpose under YHWH's covenant.

Sons of Light — the Yakhad community members in the Two Spirits doctrine. Ruled by the Angel of Light (Prince of Lights), destined for eternal life. Opposed to the Bnei Khoshekh (Sons of Darkness) in the cosmic conflict described in cols 3-4.

Sons of Darkness — in the 1QS Two Spirits doctrine, all those outside the covenant community and ruled by the Angel of Darkness. Destined for eternal destruction at the end of days. The cosmic antagonists of the Bnei Or.

Spirit of Truth — one of the two spirits YHWH placed in humanity at creation, according to 1QS cols 3-4. The Spirit of Truth rules the Sons of Light. YHWH loves the Spirit of Truth and its deeds; it leads to life. The other spirit is the Ruakh HaAvel.

Spirit of Deceit (Spirit of Injustice/Perversion) — the opposing spirit placed in humanity at creation. Rules the Sons of Darkness. Leads to the deeds of darkness and destruction. Both spirits are at war within each person until the end of days, when YHWH will purify the Sons of Light completely.

Instructor / Teacher — the community official responsible for teaching the new members, composing the community's hymns and prayers, and leading the community's wisdom traditions. The final section of 1QS (col.9-11) is a hymn and rule attributed to the Maskil. Distinguished from the Mevaqqer (Overseer) of the Damascus Document.

The Many — the full assembly of community members in 1QS. Major decisions, member disputes, and annual reviews are conducted 'before the Many.' The Many vote on admissions and punishments. The term emphasizes collective governance — no individual acts alone.

The yearly examination of every community member required by 1QS col.5: each year, every member is ranked according to their spirit and their deeds. Those who improve move up in rank; those who deteriorate move down. The ranking determines seating order at communal meals and participation in debates.

The governing council of twelve laymen and three priests specified in 1QS col.8, structured on the twelve tribes plus three priestly functions. This council is described as the foundation stone, an eternal planting, a holy of holies — the core of the community's spiritual purpose.

faq.question: What is the Two Spirits doctrine in 1QS?
faq.answer: Columns 3-4 of the Community Rule describe YHWH's creation of two spirits at the foundation of humanity: the Spirit of Truth (Ruakh HaEmet) and the Spirit of Deceit (Ruakh HaAvel). Every person is allocated a portion of each spirit, though the Sons of Light are dominated by the Spirit of Truth and the Sons of Darkness by the Spirit of Deceit. The Prince of Lights rules the Sons of Light; the Angel of Darkness rules the Sons of Darkness. All of human life — the battle between right and wrong conduct — is the working out of this cosmic conflict within and between people. At the end of days, YHWH will purify the Sons of Light completely.

faq.question: How does someone enter the Qumran Yahad?
faq.answer: Entry is a multi-year process documented in 1QS cols 5-7. A candidate presents themselves to the Overseer (Mevaqqer), who examines their spirit and deeds. If accepted, the candidate begins a period of instruction but does not yet share in communal meals or property. After the first year, the Many vote on whether to advance the candidate. After a second year of full participation in community life — but still separate from the full communal property pool — the Many vote again. Only after this probation does the member's property merge fully into the communal fund and they receive full standing in the assembly.

faq.question: What does Yakhad mean and why is it significant?
faq.answer: Yakhad means 'unity' or 'together.' The community took this as its self-designation — they were the community of the Yakhad, defined by their total collective commitment. Members shared all property, shared meals, ranked together at assembly, and were accountable to one another. The name signals that individual identity was inseparable from communal identity. This is a sharper form of communal covenant than the Damascus Document's camp communities, where members maintained individual households.

faq.question: What is the role of the Maskil?
faq.answer: The Maskil (Instructor) is the spiritual and educational leader of the community described in 1QS cols 3 and 9-11. The Maskil teaches all Sons of Light the Two Spirits doctrine — the nature of humanity, the conflict of the two spirits, and the deeds appropriate to each. The final section of 1QS (cols 9-11) is attributed to the Maskil: a rule for how the Instructor should conduct himself — speaking truth, keeping counsel, understanding timing, and composing hymns of praise for YHWH. The Maskil is not the same as the Teacher of Righteousness; the Teacher was a historical founder figure, the Maskil is a continuing office.

faq.question: What is the annual review and what are its consequences?
faq.answer: Every year the full assembly (the Many) reviews each member's spirit and deeds. Members are ranked by understanding — those who have grown in knowledge and righteous conduct move up; those who have deteriorated move down. The ranking is not abstract: it determines where a member sits at communal meals, the order in which they speak in debates, and their authority within the community. This creates a living meritocracy of covenant obedience — not based on birth, wealth, or tribal origin alone, but on how a person lives the covenant year by year.

faq.question: What does the community await according to 1QS col.9?
faq.answer: 1QS col.9 says the community conducts itself according to these rules 'until the coming of the Prophet and the Messiahs of Aaron and Israel.' Three figures are expected: a Prophet (echoing Devarim 18 and Mosheh's promise of a coming prophet), a priestly Messiah of Aharon (the anointed high priest of the final era), and a royal Messiah of Yisra'el (the anointed king). This two-Messiah framework — priestly and royal — is distinct from the later Christian single-Messiah framework. The community lived in a holding pattern, maintaining covenant purity until these figures would appear.

faq.question: How does property work in the Yahad community?
faq.answer: Full communal property sharing — the most distinctive feature of the Yahad compared to the Damascus Document camps. Upon completing the two-year probation, a new member's property becomes the property of the Many, managed by the Overseer. No member holds private property separate from the community. Violations — lying about property, taking more than one's share — are treated as serious covenant breaches subject to punishment. The One Rule (1QS col.6) explicitly states: 'No man of the members of the community shall give any of the property of the community into the hand of a man of falsehood.'

faq.question: What offenses lead to expulsion from the Yahad?
faq.answer: The 1QS penal code (cols 6-7) lists graduated punishments. Lesser offenses — speaking foolishly, interrupting a fellow, falling asleep in an assembly, bearing a grudge against a brother — lead to temporary reductions in food rations or exclusion from the pure food for set periods. Serious offenses — deliberate violation of a Mosaic commandment, betrayal of the community to outsiders, blaspheming YHWH's Name — lead to permanent expulsion. A permanently expelled member may never return. The gradation reflects the distinction between human weakness and deliberate rebellion.

faq.question: How does the Two Spirits doctrine differ from later Christian ideas?
faq.answer: The 1QS Two Spirits doctrine frames the cosmic conflict as two spirits that YHWH created and placed in humanity, with every person carrying a portion of each. This is not Persian dualism — YHWH created both spirits and rules over both. The Angel of Darkness's power exists because YHWH permits it, not as a rival deity. The NT borrowed its Spirit/flesh and light/darkness language from traditions like 1QS — the ancient text is the source; the NT adapted what was already there. The 1QS framework also does not demonize the material world itself — the conflict is between obedience and rebellion, not between matter and spirit.

faq.question: What is the significance of the Council of twelve laymen and three priests?
faq.answer: The twelve laymen echo the twelve tribes of Yisra'el — the full covenant people. The three priests echo the three priestly families (Aharon, Eleazar, Itamar) or the three patriarchs. Together the fifteen form the foundational council, described as 'an eternal planting, a holy of holies, witnesses of truth for judgment, and the chosen of lovingkindness appointed to atone for the land.' The council is the community's spiritual foundation — the reason the Yahad's covenant life has cosmic significance: they stand in for the purified covenant people, maintaining YHWH's purposes even while Jerusalem is corrupt.
